classification.tone: Raucous, profane, satirical, and emotionally pointed

evaluation.positioning_hook: After a blackout assault is buried by campus bureaucracy, a sorority girl and her grocery-store best friend infiltrate a predatory frat by posing as men to force a confession.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built around a high-recognition college-world engine, with a revenge-forward emotional promise that should travel. The hook is strongest for younger adult audiences and buyers who want a bold, conversation-starting comedy with a social edge.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The assault, the Title 9 dead end, and the cross-dressed infiltration all land early and cleanly, so the story engine is easy to explain in one breath. The script keeps returning to the same clear objective: get Brad to confess and expose the house.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Daisy and Maddy are a strong comic duo with distinct energies — Daisy’s wounded determination and Maddy’s blunt, feral loyalty play off each other well. Brad, Courtney, Tanner, Jake, and Stephanie all add playable contrast, though the script is most magnetic when the central friendship is driving.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The gender-disguise infiltration inside a frat hazing machine gives the script a confident comic engine, and the way it folds assault accountability into a party-movie structure is a sharp choice. The writing is willing to go hard on humiliation, performance, and social codes, which gives it a distinct comic identity.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps resetting the objective with fresh tactics — Title 9, the rush plan, the mic setup, the Jungle party, the final confrontation — so it rarely sits still. A few stretches lean on repeated infiltration beats, but the escalation into the finale keeps the page-turn energy alive.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This is a familiar campus-comedy arena, but the specific collision of assault aftermath, frat-bro performance, and female friendship-as-ops-team gives it a fresh, inevitable shape. The idea of women weaponizing the same social theater that protects the frat is the kind of premise that feels both new and instantly understandable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Greek life is rendered as a full social ecosystem with rituals, status games, hazing logic, party hierarchies, and campus bureaucracy all feeding the story. The Market Basket, sorority house, Title 9 office, and frat house each carry their own behavioral rules, which makes the world feel story-generating rather than decorative.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific comic voice: filthy, fast, self-aware, and emotionally sincere when it needs to be. It can pivot from absurd frat-bro banter to real anger and humiliation without losing its identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the prank-war structure, the script keeps revealing deeper material about belief, complicity, female solidarity, and how social systems train people to doubt themselves. The ending’s campus-wide fallout and the friendship repair suggest a larger emotional afterlife beyond the immediate plot.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Daisy/Maddy is a strong lead partnership, and the supporting web around them — Tanner, Courtney, Stephanie, Jake, Brad, the frat brothers, the sorority sisters — creates multiple playable pairings. The script repeatedly generates scenes where any two characters in the orbit can produce comedy, conflict, or revelation.

casting_characteristics: Cross-dressed / disguise sequences for Daisy and Maddy
One adult supporting role in Tanner

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with frequent campus and party exteriors
notable_requirements: Bedroom, basement, bathroom, and party spaces

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond simple title cards and montage-style transitions.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical vomit, fire gag on wig, beer spills, brand-mark makeup/prosthetics, and a few physical comedy beats.

rights_flags.detail: Multiple named or clearly referenced songs and artists are used as tone markers, including John Mayer, Troye Sivan, Chappell Roan, Waka Flocka, and Mo Bamba-style party cues.
Brand and product references appear throughout, including Jose Cuervo, Market Basket, Zara, McKinsey, Whole Foods, and various college-party consumer markers.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Streaming feature / premium cable comedy lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release with strong festival-to-streaming or direct-streaming potential

cost.note: Contemporary college settings, a contained house-and-campus footprint, and practical effects keep the budget in a modest feature range.

cast.note: The script needs a strong two-lead package plus a sizable college ensemble, with several roles that benefit from sharp comic casting.

location.note: The story moves through a handful of recurring locations, but the frat, sorority, campus, and party spaces all need to feel distinct and active.

content.note: Sexual assault, drugging, explicit language, hazing, and nudity-adjacent party material narrow the lane to mature buyers.

rights.note: The script uses several named songs and brands, plus real-world campus-administration language that would need standard clearance review.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise weaponizes frat culture from inside.
strengths.what_it_means: This gives producers a clean, marketable engine: a revenge comedy that turns the frat’s own rituals, language, and status games against it. Buyers looking for a sharp, youth-facing satire with a built-in social conversation will recognize the hook immediately.
strengths.evidence: Daisy and Maddy infiltrate Delta by dressing as guys, learning the code, and using rush, hazing, and brotherhood against Brad.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Daisy and Maddy are a strong comic duo.
strengths.what_it_means: The central friendship gives the movie emotional traction and a repeatable scene engine, because each woman brings a different tactic, rhythm, and worldview. Casting directors will see two roles that can anchor a breakout pair of young leads or a star-plus-discovery combo.
strengths.evidence: Their ping-pong banter, grocery-store tag-team, secret handshake, and constant tactical bickering all define the movie’s rhythm.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a clear, propulsive objective.
strengths.what_it_means: The story always knows what it is trying to do — get Brad to confess and expose the house — which makes it easy to pitch and easy to follow. That clarity is a major asset for buyers who want a commercial comedy with a social spine rather than a loose hangout movie.
strengths.evidence: Title 9, the rush infiltration, the mic plan, the Jungle setup, and the final confession all serve the same goal.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Greek life is rendered as a full ecosystem.
strengths.what_it_means: The world has enough internal rules, status ladders, and social rituals to support a feature with real texture and repeat-view value. Streamers and indie buyers alike respond to settings that feel specific enough to generate scenes on their own.
strengths.evidence: Rush, pledging, Nationals, Honor Council, Tiki Bar access, brother-only spaces, and sorority politics all operate as story mechanics.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The tone can swing from filthy to sincere.
strengths.what_it_means: That tonal range broadens the audience beyond pure shock comedy, because the movie can deliver laughs while still landing the emotional reality of being disbelieved. It’s the kind of tonal control that attracts directors who want to balance provocation with heart.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from vomit gags and sock-dicks to the Title 9 office, Daisy’s breakdown, and the final confession.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Courtney and Stephanie widen the emotional field.
strengths.what_it_means: These supporting women keep the movie from becoming a two-hander by adding a second female lane of conflict, alliance, and repair. That gives the project more casting appeal and more audience entry points than a simple revenge setup.
strengths.evidence: Courtney shifts from antagonist to ally, and Stephanie moves from romantic subplot to campus solidarity and self-defense leadership.

whats_special.headline: RUSH has the kind of high-contrast commercial engine that gets attention fast: a filthy, propulsive campus comedy built around two women who infiltrate a frat’s own masculinity theater to expose what it protects. It’s funny, specific, and built on a premise that can sell in one sentence while still carrying real emotional and cultural charge.

lead_characters.name: DAISY
lead_characters.hook: Daisy is a bright, socially fluent freshman who starts the movie as the campus version of a golden girl and ends it as someone forced to decide whether belonging is worth self-erasure. She’s funny, wounded, and more strategic than she first appears, with a core contradiction between wanting to be loved by the system and wanting to burn it down.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Kaitlyn Dever in *Booksmart* or Carey Mulligan in *Promising Young Woman* — a role that can pivot from comic ease to fury, humiliation, and moral clarity without losing control. Young actresses looking for a breakout lead with range, edge, and a real emotional spine will chase this.

lead_characters.name: MADDY
lead_characters.hook: Maddy is Daisy’s grocery-store best friend: blunt, masc, funny, and allergic to polite social performance. She reads as the outsider who sees through the whole campus machine, but the script lets her become the one who understands how to play it better than anyone else.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Ayo Edebiri had in *Bottoms* or Rachel Sennott had in *Shiva Baby* — a fast-talking, high-precision comic part that also carries loyalty, desire, and surprise. Actors with sharp comedic timing and a little edge will want the chance to make this character iconic.

lead_characters.name: BRAD
lead_characters.hook: Brad is the movie’s charismatic predator: handsome, socially fluent, and always one step away from turning cruelty into charm. He’s built to be seductive in public and monstrous in private, which makes him a strong comic-villain engine and a real audience target.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role Jacob Elordi had in *Saltburn* or Penn Badgley had in *You* — a polished, dangerous presence who can weaponize likability. Actors who want to play a handsome antagonist with real scene-stealing power will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: TANNER
lead_characters.hook: Tanner is Maddy’s older brother and the movie’s accidental mentor: a reformed frat guy who still speaks the language of male performance but has enough self-awareness to help the girls game the system. He’s funny because he’s both ridiculous and useful, a guy who wants to reconnect with his boys while quietly being outgrown by them.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the comic-supporting lane of Paul Rudd in *I Love You, Man* or Adam Scott in *Step Brothers* — a role that gets laughs by being both competent and emotionally stranded. Actors who can play deadpan authority with a soft center will want it.

lead_characters.name: STEPHANIE
lead_characters.hook: Stephanie is the ethereal sorority girl who starts as a romantic object and becomes one of the movie’s clearest moral witnesses. She’s smart, socially legible, and unexpectedly grounded, which lets the script use her to puncture assumptions about who sees what and who gets believed.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Zoey Deutch a showcase in *Set It Up* or Haley Lu Richardson in *The Edge of Seventeen* — charming, readable, and capable of shifting from flirtation to moral clarity in a beat. Young actresses with warmth and comic timing will see real value here.

lead_characters.name: JAKE
lead_characters.hook: Jake is the soft-boy freshman who keeps trying to be sincere inside a system built on posturing. He starts as a cute distraction and ends up as a useful mirror for how easily male passivity becomes complicity.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the awkward-romantic lane of Lucas Hedges in *Lady Bird* or Justice Smith in *The Get Down* — a role that gets its charm from vulnerability, confusion, and emotional openness. Actors who can play sweet, funny, and slightly lost will want this part.

lead_characters.name: COURTNEY
lead_characters.hook: Courtney begins as the polished girlfriend who seems to own the social hierarchy, then reveals a sharper, more wounded intelligence underneath. She’s the kind of character who can move from status to solidarity without feeling like a different person.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the pivot Olivia Wilde did in *Booksmart* or Emma Roberts in *Scream 4* — glamorous surface, then a real turn into self-knowledge and alliance. Actors who want a part with bite and a late-emerging conscience will be interested.

lead_characters.name: HARRISON
lead_characters.hook: Harrison is the frat president who treats absurdity like governance and governance like a joke. He’s a comic institutional face for the house, the guy who can make the frat feel like a functioning bureaucracy of nonsense.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that gives an actor the dry authority of a *Veep* operator or a *21 Jump Street* campus alpha — a chance to play power as performance. Character actors with sharp timing will have fun making him memorable.

lead_characters.name: OLIVIA
lead_characters.hook: Olivia is one of Daisy’s sorority friends, initially more reactive than active, but she becomes part of the movie’s female network once the truth is undeniable. She helps widen the campus response from private pain to collective action.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of ensemble-support role that works like the best parts in *Mean Girls* or *Bottoms* — a sharp, specific friend who helps define the social world. Young comic actors will see a clean lane to make the character pop in limited screen time.

lead_characters.name: KENDALL
lead_characters.hook: Kendall is the other half of Daisy’s early social orbit, a girl who starts out complicit in the campus hierarchy and gradually becomes part of the correction. She’s useful because she can play both shallow social reflex and genuine remorse.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a classic ensemble-support slot with room for a sharp comic actress to turn a familiar campus type into something more human. It has the kind of quick-turn material that actors use to stand out in a crowded cast.

lead_characters.name: THEO
lead_characters.hook: Theo is the film-bro philosopher who thinks he’s above the frat while still living inside it. He’s a great comic pressure valve because he can be pretentious, horny, and oddly sincere in the same breath.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the deadpan self-regard of a *Parks and Recreation* or *The White Lotus* hanger-on — a chance to make pretension funny without flattening the character. Scene-stealing supporting players will want it.

lead_characters.name: ANGELO
lead_characters.hook: Angelo is the social glue of the frat, the guy who is always in the conversation and always trying to keep the vibe alive. He’s less ideological than the others, which makes him useful as a barometer for how groupthink spreads.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong ensemble-support part in the vein of the best hangout-movie sidekicks — a role that lets an actor play charm, insecurity, and herd instinct at once. It’s the kind of part that can become a fan favorite if cast right.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a savage campus comedy with real emotional teeth.
director_appeal.fit_profile: First- or second-feature directors, or indie-comedy directors with one or two festival titles, who already work in performance-forward material and can stage ensemble chaos without losing clarity. This material rewards directors who like social satire, bodily comedy, and scenes that turn on power shifts rather than spectacle.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a chance to choreograph a large, talky ensemble while still landing a clean emotional arc for the lead pair. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who want to prove they can handle provocation, pace, and tonal control in one package.

buyer_appeal.detail: The project can be packaged around two breakout young leads and a strong supporting ensemble, so it does not require a tentpole-level cast to work. The college setting, contained locations, and topical premise fit the current buyer appetite for youth-skewing, conversation-driving features that can travel well on streaming.

considerations.area: The confession engine can be sharpened earlier.
considerations.detail: The script is strongest when Daisy and Maddy are actively engineering the Brad trap, and a next pass could foreground that objective a little sooner after the Title 9 scene. What would it look like if the audience felt the endgame tightening even before the rush disguise kicks in?

The rush sequence, the guy-disguise training, the first failed Brad encounter, and the later party infiltration all play in the same comic lane. One lever would be to collapse one of those beats or let one scene do double duty so the escalation feels even more vertical.

considerations.area: The supporting women could carry more independent motion.
considerations.detail: Courtney, Olivia, and Kendall become important once the campus response turns collective, and the version of the script where they each have one more decisive action would deepen the ensemble engine. That would also make the final campus-wide payoff feel even more earned.

considerations.area: The music and brand references need a clearance pass.
considerations.detail: The script uses several named songs, artists, and consumer brands as tone markers, so a production would want to swap or clear those elements early. The upside is that the contemporary party-world texture is already doing a lot of the work, so the story can survive those substitutions cleanly.

considerations.area: The party nights will want disciplined scheduling.
considerations.detail: The Jungle sequence, the frat parties, and the night exteriors create the bulk of the shoot’s logistical load. A production-minded pass could group those scenes tightly so the movie keeps its energy without spreading the night work across too many company moves.
